prize_parts.citation: For developing empirical methods to estimate demand, market power and competition in differentiated-product industries with endogenous prices.

statement.case_for: Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes (1995) solved a concrete problem: how to estimate substitution patterns and market power in differentiated-product markets when prices are endogenous. The solution became the standard instrument of empirical industrial organisation, and it also spread into trade, health and environmental economics. It is used routinely in merger review and antitrust, so the measurement is tied to real policy counterfactuals. The core work is 30 years old and has been scrutinised, extended and re-implemented in many settings, so there is no maturity question. Attribution is also relatively clean for the demand side: the BLP estimator is identified with these three names. Pakes adds the dynamic-industry line (Ericson-Pakes) and the estimation of dynamic oligopoly. I still rank this first after the discussion. The colleagues' arguments for B009 and B014 persuade me those are strong, mature candidates, and I keep both as alternatives. They do not change my view that B045 offers the most clearly attributable and most widely transferred methodological advance on the list.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. The three-name cap leaves out Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin, and Bresnahan has an independent claim to the earlier structural IO agenda. Pakes's dynamic-games work and the BLP demand system are two related but distinct contributions, so a citation that covers both may be too broad or too thin. The case is also mainly methodological. Several colleagues put B045 low (Krusell 8th, Strömberg and Enflo 5th) and ranked B009 and B014 higher, and the opening evidence for B045 is narrower. Identification and instrument-validity critiques of BLP exist, although they have not displaced the approach.

responses.point: Ranked B045 eighth and asked whether it is a narrower methods prize than the macro and labour candidates above it.
responses.response: Narrowness of topic is not the right test. The question is whether the method changed what can be measured and decided. BLP made it possible to quantify market power, merger effects and welfare from market data, and agencies and academics now do this routinely. I accept that a method needs to be tied to findings, which it is here through merger and regulatory practice. But I do not accept that a methods prize ranks below a discovery prize by default, and your own scale for B009 and B025 values the same kind of downstream use. I would have more doubts if the citation covered only the technique. That is why I keep it to demand estimation and competition.

responses.point: Ranked B045 third and flagged that as an IO specialist he may weight this field more heavily than others would. He sees a trade-off between honouring the BLP method and the broader structural IO agenda.
responses.response: I take the caveat seriously, and I do not think specialist familiarity should count as merit. My ranking rests on the evidence of use outside IO and on three decades of confirmation. I agree with your trade-off, and I resolve it toward the BLP trio. That is the narrowest set of names that credits the demand estimator cleanly, and it still carries Pakes's dynamic line. A broader structural-IO prize would honour Bresnahan and Reiss, but it would turn a fairly crisp attribution into a research-programme prize. The cap makes that costly.

responses.point: Ranked B009 first with Autor, Hanson and Dorn on the China-shock strand, and said the credit boundary with Katz and the task framework is contestable.
responses.response: I agree the boundary for B009 is genuinely contestable. The China-shock strand points to Autor, Dorn and Hanson, while Katz anchors the wage-structure and skill-supply work. A three-name cap forces a choice of which strand to credit, and I do not think that choice is easy. That is part of why I rank B009 below B045 on attribution. B009 is nonetheless a very strong alternative, and I would support it if the committee were to resolve the Dorn-or-Katz choice convincingly. B045 has a similar problem in Bresnahan, but there the BLP estimator is identified with a single trio.

responses.point: Ranked B009 first. He cites replication, transparent identification and policy relevance, and flags overlap with the 2023 and 2024 prizes and the exclusion of Dorn.
responses.response: I agree with your account of the evidence. B009 is mature, replicated and policy-relevant, and I ranked it third. My hesitation is the overlap you point to with the Goldin and Acemoglu awards and the Dorn-versus-Katz choice. Identification of the shift-share designs is also still debated. Those concerns lower the marginal case for B009 without removing it. B045 carries no comparable overlap with a recent prize, which is why I keep it first while treating B009 as the most credible rival.

uncertainties: Whether the committee would credit Bresnahan in place of Levinsohn, or add him alongside Berry and Pakes, and the attribution consequences.
Whether the citation should cover only demand estimation or also Pakes's dynamic-industry work, and whether combining them fits one coherent discovery.
Whether the committee will treat this as a primarily methodological prize and weigh it differently from discovery-based candidates.
Whether B009's Dorn-or-Katz attribution can be resolved convincingly enough for it to be the stronger candidate.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for the credited B045 names. The profile documents SSE affiliation alongside committee colleagues Dreber Almenberg, Friberg and Strömberg. That is a collegial tie, not a connection to any candidate, and I disclose it without adjudicating. My own work is in market and mechanism design and does not overlap with the B045 authors according to the profile.
